There were many lamps burning upstairs where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting in a window. As Paul kept speaking, Eutychus grew drowsier and fell into a deep sleep. He fell from the third floor and was picked up dead.
Paul went down, bent over him, and held him close. “Don’t panic,” he said. “He’s alive.”
Paul went back upstairs, broke bread and ate. He talked with them for a long time, until daybreak, and then left.
They took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.
We went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we planned to pick up Paul. He had arranged to go there by land.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went to Mitylene.
The next day we sailed across from Chios. The day after that we reached Samos, stayed at Trogyllium, and the following day arrived in Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so he wouldn’t lose time in Asia. He was hurrying to reach Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church to meet him.
When they arrived, he said, “You know how I lived among you from the first day I came to Asia.
“I served the Lord with humility, with many tears, and through the troubles caused by the Jews’ plots against me.
“I never held back from telling you anything that would help you. I taught you in public and from house to house.
“I urged both Jews and Greeks to turn to God and trust in our Lord Jesus.
“Now I’m going to Jerusalem, compelled by the Spirit, though I don’t know what will happen to me there.
“I only know that in every city the Holy Spirit warns me that prison and suffering are waiting for me.
“But my life isn’t what I’m focused on. I want to finish my course with joy and complete the ministry the Lord Jesus gave me: to testify to the Good News of God’s grace.
“Now I know none of you, among whom I traveled announcing God’s Kingdom, will see me again.
“So I declare to you today that I’m not responsible for anyone’s blood,
“because I never held back from telling you everything God wants you to know.
“Watch out for yourselves and for the whole flock. The Holy Spirit made you its overseers. Shepherd the church of the Lord and God, which he bought with his own blood.
“I know that after I leave, savage wolves will come among you and won’t spare the flock.
“Even some of you will twist the truth to draw disciples after yourselves.
“So stay alert. Remember that for three years I kept warning each of you night and day, often with tears.
“Now I entrust you to God and to his message of grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all who are set apart for God.
“I never wanted anyone’s silver, gold, or clothing.
“You know that these hands provided for my needs and for the people with me.
“In everything I did, I showed you that by working hard we should help the weak. Remember the Lord Jesus’ words: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
After saying this, Paul knelt down and prayed with them all.
They all wept openly, hugged Paul, and kissed him goodbye.
They were especially sad because he had said they would never see him again. Then they walked with him to the ship.
After saying goodbye, we sailed straight to Cos. The next day we reached Rhodes, and from there Patara.
We found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, boarded it, and sailed away.
We came into view of Cyprus, passed it to our left, and sailed on to Syria. We landed at Tyre, where the ship was unloading its cargo.
We found the disciples there and stayed seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
When our time there was up, we continued the journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, came with us outside the city. We knelt on the beach and prayed together.
After saying goodbye, we boarded the ship, and they went back home.
We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the believers there and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
We had been there for several days when a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came over, took Paul’s belt, tied his own feet and hands with it, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘This is how the Jews in Jerusalem will tie up the man who owns this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”
When we heard this, we and the local believers begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
But Paul answered, “Why are you crying and breaking my heart? I’m ready not only to be tied up in Jerusalem but also to die there for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he wouldn’t be persuaded, we stopped arguing and said, “May the Lord’s will be done.”
After those days, we packed up and went to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea went with us and brought us to Mnason from Cyprus, an early disciple, whose home would host us.
When we reached Jerusalem, the believers welcomed us warmly.
The next day Paul went with us to see James, and all the elders were there.
After greeting them, Paul gave a detailed report of what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard it, they praised God. Then they said to Paul, “Brother, you can see that thousands of Jews have believed, and they are all deeply committed to the Law.
“They’ve been told that you teach Jews living among the Gentiles to abandon Moses—that you tell them not to circumcise their children or follow our customs.
“What should we do? They will certainly hear that you’ve arrived, and the whole group will come together.
“So do what we tell you. Four men here have taken a vow.

“Go with them and complete the purification rite. Pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know the reports about you aren’t true and that you also live in obedience to the Law.
“As for Gentile believers, we have sent them our decision: they should avoid food sacrificed to idols, blood, meat from strangled animals, and sexual immorality.”

The next day Paul took the men and joined them in the purification rite. Then he went into the temple to announce when the days of purification would end and the offering would be made for each of them.
When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from Asia saw Paul in the temple. They stirred up the crowd and seized him.

They shouted, “People of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people, the Law, and this place. He has even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place!”
They had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up. People rushed together, grabbed Paul, and dragged him out of the temple. The doors were shut at once.
As the crowd was trying to kill Paul, word reached the Roman commander that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
He immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the commander and soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came over, arrested Paul, and ordered him chained with two chains. Then he asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one accusation, others another. Since the noise made it impossible to learn the facts, the commander ordered Paul taken to the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because the crowd was so violent.
The crowd followed, shouting, “Get rid of him!”
As Paul was about to be taken into the barracks, he asked the commander, “May I say something to you?” The commander replied, “You speak Greek?
“Aren’t you the Egyptian who recently started a revolt and led four thousand men of the Assassins into the wilderness?”
Paul answered, “I’m a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of a respected city. Please let me speak to the people.”
When the commander gave him permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand for the crowd to be quiet. When they fell silent, he spoke to them in Hebrew.
Brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I’m making to you now.
When they heard him speaking to them in Hebrew, they grew even quieter. Then he said:

“I’m a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but I grew up here in this city. I studied at Gamaliel’s feet and was trained carefully in the law handed down by our ancestors. I was zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I hunted down the people of this Way to the point of death. I arrested both men and women and put them in prison.

The high priest and the whole council of elders can confirm this. They gave me letters for our fellow Jews, and I went to Damascus to arrest the believers there and bring them back to Jerusalem for punishment.
“As I traveled and came close to Damascus, around noon a bright light from heaven suddenly flashed all around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice say, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’
I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ He told me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, the one you are persecuting.’
The people with me saw the light and were frightened, but they didn’t understand the voice speaking to me.
I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘Get up and go into Damascus. There you’ll be told everything God has appointed you to do.’
I couldn’t see because the light was so brilliant, so my companions led me by the hand into Damascus.
A man named Ananias came to me. He was devoted to the law and respected by all the Jews living in Damascus.
He stood beside me and said, ‘Brother Saul, see again!’ At that very moment, I looked up and could see him.
He said, ‘The God our ancestors worshiped chose you to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear his voice.
You’ll be his witness to everyone, telling them what you’ve seen and heard.
So what are you waiting for? Get up, be baptized, and have your sins washed away as you call on the Lord’s name.’
“Later, after I returned to Jerusalem, I was praying in the temple when I fell into a trance.
I saw the Lord telling me, ‘Leave Jerusalem quickly. They won’t accept your testimony about me.’
I said, ‘Lord, they know I went through the synagogues, throwing believers in prison and beating them.
When Stephen, your witness, was killed, I stood there approving. I even watched the clothes of the men who murdered him.’
“But the Lord said to me, ‘Go. I’m sending you far away to the Gentiles.’”
The crowd listened until he said that. Then they shouted, “Get rid of this man! He shouldn’t be allowed to live!”
They kept shouting, waving their cloaks around and throwing dust into the air.
The commander ordered Paul taken into the barracks. He told the soldiers to question him under a whipping, trying to find out why the crowd was yelling like this.
As they stretched him out to tie him for the whipping, Paul asked the centurion standing nearby, “Is it lawful to whip a Roman citizen who hasn’t been found guilty?”
When the centurion heard that, he went to the commander and warned him, “Be careful what you do. This man is a Roman citizen!”
The commander came to Paul and asked, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” Paul said, “Yes.”
The commander replied, “I paid a lot for my citizenship.” Paul said, “I was born a citizen.”
Right away, the men who were about to question Paul backed off. The commander was alarmed when he realized he had put a Roman citizen in chains.

The next day, the commander wanted to learn exactly why the Jews were accusing Paul. He released him from his chains and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to meet. Then he brought Paul down and set him before them.
Paul looked straight at the council and said, “Brothers, I’ve lived before God with a clear conscience right up to today.”
At that, the high priest Ananias ordered the men standing near Paul to hit him on the mouth.
Paul said to him, “God will strike you, you polished-up wall! You’re sitting there to judge me by the law, yet you order me struck in violation of the law.”
The men standing nearby said, “You dare insult God’s high priest?”
Paul said, “Brothers, I didn’t realize he was the high priest. Scripture says, ‘You must not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

Paul knew that some of the council were Sadducees and others were Pharisees, so he called out, “Brothers, I’m a Pharisee, from a family of Pharisees. I’m on trial because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead!”
As soon as he said this, the Pharisees and Sadducees began arguing, and the council split into opposing sides.
The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, no angels, and no spirits, while the Pharisees believe in all of them.

The shouting grew intense. Some of the Pharisee scribes stood up and argued, “We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel really did speak to him? We shouldn’t fight against God!”
The argument became so fierce that the commander feared they would tear Paul apart. He ordered the soldiers to pull him out of the crowd by force and take him back to the barracks.
That night the Lord stood beside Paul and said, “Be encouraged! You’ve testified about me here in Jerusalem, and you must testify about me in Rome too.”
When morning came, some of the Jews formed a plot and put themselves under an oath: they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
More than forty men were part of this plot.
They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We’ve taken a serious oath not to eat anything until Paul is dead.
So now you and the council should ask the commander to bring Paul down to you tomorrow, as if you want to examine his case more carefully. We’ll be ready to kill him before he gets here.”
But the son of Paul’s sister heard that they were waiting in ambush. He went into the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander. He has something to report.”
The centurion brought him to the commander and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you. He has something to tell you.”
The commander took the young man by the hand, stepped aside with him, and asked privately, “What do you need to tell me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, pretending they want to investigate his case more carefully.
“Don’t agree to it. More than forty men are hiding in wait for him. They’ve sworn not to eat or drink until they’ve killed him. They’re ready now, just waiting for you to say yes.”
The commander sent the young man away with a warning: “Don’t tell anyone that you brought this information to me.”
He called two centurions and said, “Get two hundred soldiers ready to go to Caesarea, along with seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen. Leave at the third hour of the night.
“Provide horses for Paul as well, and get him safely to Governor Felix.”
Then he wrote a letter that said:
“Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix: Greetings.
“This man was seized by the Jews, who were about to kill him. I came with my troops and rescued him after learning that he was a Roman citizen.
“I wanted to know what charge they were bringing against him, so I took him before their council.
“I found that their accusations were about questions of their law. He wasn’t accused of anything deserving death or imprisonment.
“When I was informed that a plot was being made against him, I sent him to you at once. I also ordered his accusers to bring their case before you. Farewell.”
The soldiers followed their orders and took Paul by night as far as Antipatris.
The next day the foot soldiers returned to the barracks, leaving the cavalry to continue with him.
When the cavalry reached Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and handed Paul over to him.
The governor read the letter and asked which province Paul came from. When he learned that Paul was from Cilicia,
he said, “I’ll hear your case fully when your accusers arrive.” Then he ordered Paul held in Herod’s palace.
Five days later, the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus. They presented their case against Paul to the governor. ⚖️
Paul was called in, and Tertullus began accusing him: “Governor Felix, because of your leadership this nation enjoys much peace, and your wise decisions keep making life better. 👑
“We welcome this in every way and everywhere, most excellent Felix, with deep gratitude. 🙏
“But I do not want to take up too much of your time. Please hear us out briefly. ⏳
“We have found this man to be a public menace, stirring up riots among Jews everywhere and leading the Nazarene sect. ⚠️
“He even tried to defile the temple, so we arrested him. 🏛️
“If you examine him yourself, you can confirm all the things we are accusing him of.” 🔎
The other Jews joined in, claiming these charges were true. 🗣️
The governor nodded for Paul to speak. Paul answered, “I know you have judged this nation for many years, so I am glad to defend myself before you. 🙋
“You can check that I arrived in Jerusalem no more than twelve days ago to worship. 📆
“They did not find me arguing with anyone or stirring up a crowd in the temple, the synagogues, or anywhere in the city. 🏛️
“And they cannot prove the things they are accusing me of now. ⚖️
“But I admit this: I worship the God of our ancestors according to the Way they call a sect. I believe everything written in the Law and the Prophets. 📖
“I share the same hope in God that these men have: that the dead—both the righteous and the unrighteous—will rise again. 🌅
“That is why I work hard to keep my conscience clear before God and people at all times. 💛
“After several years away, I returned to bring gifts for the poor among my people and offerings. 🎁
“I was purified in the temple when some Jews from Asia found me. There was no crowd and no disturbance. 🕊️
“Those men should be here in court to accuse me if they have anything against me. 👀
“Or these people here can say what wrong they found when I stood before the council. ⚖️
“Unless it was about one thing I shouted: ‘I am on trial before you today because I believe the dead will rise!’” 📣
Felix knew the Way fairly well, so he postponed the hearing. “I will decide your case when Commander Lysias arrives,” he said. ⏳
He ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard but give him some freedom and not stop his friends from caring for or visiting him. 🔓
A few days later, Felix came with his Jewish wife Drusilla. He sent for Paul and listened as Paul spoke about faith in Christ Jesus. 🗣️
As Paul talked about doing what is right, self-control, and the coming judgment, Felix became afraid. “That is enough for now. Go. I will call for you when it is convenient.” 😨
Felix also hoped Paul would offer him money for a release. So he sent for Paul often and talked with him. 🪙
After two years, Porcius Festus took Felix’s place. Wanting to gain favor with the Jews, Felix left Paul in prison. ⛓️
Three days after Festus arrived in the province, he went from Caesarea up to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and Jewish leaders brought their charges against Paul to him and urged him,
asking him to do them a favor by sending Paul to Jerusalem. They were plotting to kill Paul along the way.
Festus replied that Paul would stay in custody at Caesarea and that he himself would soon go there.
He said, “Let your leaders come down with me. If the man has done anything wrong, they can bring charges against him.”
After staying with them more than ten days, Festus went down to Caesarea. The next day he took his seat on the judgment bench and ordered Paul brought in.
When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come from Jerusalem surrounded him and brought many serious charges they couldn’t prove.
Paul defended himself: “I haven’t done anything wrong against the Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar.”
But Festus wanted to gain favor with the Jews, so he asked Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there before me on these charges?”
Paul said, “I’m standing before Caesar’s court, where I should be tried. I haven’t wronged the Jews, as you know very well.
If I’ve done something wrong that deserves death, I don’t refuse to die. But if their charges against me aren’t true, no one can hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
After conferring with his council, Festus answered, “You’ve appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you’ll go.”
Some days later, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived in Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
Since they stayed there many days, Festus discussed Paul’s case with the king. He said, “There’s a man Felix left in prison.
When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and Jewish elders brought charges against him and asked me to condemn him.
I told them it isn’t Roman custom to hand anyone over before the accused meets the accusers face to face and gets a chance to defend himself against the charges.
So when they came here, I didn’t delay. The very next day I took my seat on the judgment bench and ordered the man brought in.
When his accusers stood up, they didn’t charge him with the crimes I had expected.
They only had arguments with him about their religion and about a man named Jesus, who had died but whom Paul claimed was alive.
I was confused about how to investigate these matters, so I asked Paul if he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there.
But Paul appealed to remain in custody for the emperor’s decision. So I ordered him kept until I could send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I’d like to hear the man myself.” Festus replied, “Tomorrow you will.”
The next day Agrippa and Bernice arrived with great ceremony and entered the audience hall with the military commanders and leading men of the city. At Festus’ command, Paul was brought in.
Festus said, “King Agrippa and everyone here with us, you see this man. The whole crowd of Jews has petitioned me about him, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he shouldn’t be allowed to live.
I found he’d done nothing deserving death. But since he appealed to the emperor, I decided to send him.
I don’t have any definite charge to write to my lord about him. That’s why I’ve brought him before all of you, especially you, King Agrippa, so that after this hearing I’ll have something to write.
It seems unreasonable to send a prisoner without stating the charges against him.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “You may speak for yourself.” So Paul stretched out his hand and began his defense.
“I consider myself fortunate, King Agrippa, to make my defense before you today against all the charges the Jews bring against me,
especially because you know all the Jewish customs and disputes. So please listen to me patiently.
“All the Jews know how I lived from my youth, from the beginning among my own people and in Jerusalem.
They’ve known me for a long time. If they’re willing to testify, they know I lived as a Pharisee, the strictest group in our religion.
Now I’m standing trial because I hope in the promise God made to our ancestors.
Our twelve tribes hope to receive that promise as they worship God earnestly day and night. It’s because of this hope, King Agrippa, that the Jews accuse me!
Why should any of you find it impossible to believe that God raises the dead?
“I myself was convinced I should oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth in every way.
That’s what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests, I locked many of God’s people in prison. When they were sentenced to death, I voted against them.
I often punished them in the synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme. I was so furious with them that I chased them down even in foreign cities.
“That’s how I came to Damascus, with authority and a commission from the chief priests.
At noon, King Agrippa, I saw a light from heaven brighter than the sun shining around me and those traveling with me.
We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice speaking to me in Hebrew: ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It’s hard for you to kick against the goads.’
I asked, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord said, ‘I am Jesus, the one you’re persecuting.
Get up and stand on your feet. I’ve appeared to you for this purpose: to appoint you as my servant and witness to what you’ve seen and what I’ll show you.
I’ll rescue you from your own people and from the Gentiles. I’m sending you to them
to open their eyes, so they may turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God. Then they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those made holy through faith in me.’
“So, King Agrippa, I didn’t disobey the vision from heaven.
I preached first in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout Judea, and also to the Gentiles. I told them to repent and turn to God, and to show that change by how they live.
That’s why the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me.
But God has helped me, and to this day I stand here testifying to everyone, both ordinary people and important ones. I’m saying nothing beyond what Moses and the Prophets said would happen:
that the Christ would suffer, and that by rising from the dead he would be the first to announce light to our people and to the Gentiles.”
As Paul said this in his defense, Festus shouted, “Paul, you’re out of your mind! All your learning is making you crazy!”
Paul replied, “I’m not crazy, most excellent Festus. I’m speaking words that are true and sensible.
The king knows about these things, and I can speak freely to him. I’m sure none of this has escaped his notice, because it didn’t happen in some hidden corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the Prophets? I know you do.”
Agrippa said to Paul, “Do you think you can persuade me so quickly to become a Christian?”
Paul answered, “Quickly or not, I pray to God that not only you but everyone listening to me today would become like me—except for these chains.”
The king stood up, along with the governor, Bernice, and the others sitting with them.
After they left, they said to each other, “This man hasn’t done anything deserving death or imprisonment.”
Agrippa told Festus, “This man could have been released if he hadn’t appealed to Caesar.”
When it was decided that we would sail for Italy, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, who belonged to the Imperial Regiment.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was about to sail for ports along the coast of Asia. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, came with us.
The next day we stopped at Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and let him visit his friends so they could provide for him.
From there we put out to sea and sailed under the sheltered side of Cyprus because the winds were against us.
After sailing across the sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we reached Myra in Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us aboard it.
We sailed slowly for many days and had difficulty reaching a point across from Cnidus. Since the wind wouldn’t let us continue that way, we sailed under the sheltered side of Crete, opposite Salmone.
We struggled along the coast and reached a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasea.
A lot of time had passed, and sailing had become dangerous because the Fast had already passed. So Paul warned them,
saying, “Men, I can see this voyage is going to bring injury and heavy loss—not only to the cargo and ship, but to our lives too.”
But the centurion trusted the ship’s captain and owner more than Paul’s warning.

Since the harbor wasn’t suitable for wintering, most people advised sailing on, hoping they could reach Phoenix and spend the winter there. Phoenix was a harbor in Crete, facing southwest and northwest.
When a gentle south wind began to blow, they thought they had what they wanted. They pulled up anchor and sailed close along the shore of Crete.
But before long, a violent wind called the Northeaster swept down from the island.
The ship was caught in the storm and couldn’t face the wind, so we gave in and were driven along.
We sailed under the shelter of a small island called Clauda and managed, with difficulty, to secure the ship’s lifeboat.
After hauling it aboard, they used ropes to reinforce the ship. Afraid they’d run aground on the sandbars of Syrtis, they lowered the sea anchor and let the wind drive us along.
The storm battered us so badly that the next day they began throwing cargo overboard.
On the third day, they threw the ship’s equipment overboard with their own hands.
For many days we saw neither sun nor stars, and the storm kept raging. At last, all hope that we’d be saved was gone.
After they’d gone a long time without food, Paul stood among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete. Then we wouldn’t have suffered this damage and loss.
But now I urge you: Take heart! None of you will lose your life. Only the ship will be lost.
Last night an angel from the God I belong to and serve stood beside me
and said, ‘Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar. And God has graciously given you everyone sailing with you.’
“So take heart, men! I trust God that it will happen just as he told me.
But we must run aground on an island.”
On the fourteenth night, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, the sailors sensed around midnight that land was near.
They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. A little later they took soundings again and found fifteen fathoms.
Afraid we’d hit rocks, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daylight.
The sailors tried to escape from the ship. They lowered the lifeboat into the sea, pretending they were going to put out anchors from the bow.
Paul told the centurion and soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.”
So the soldiers cut the lifeboat’s ropes and let it drift away.
Just before dawn, Paul urged everyone to eat. He said, “For fourteen days you’ve been waiting anxiously and going without food—you haven’t eaten anything.
So I urge you to eat something. You need it to survive. Not one of you will lose even a hair from your head.”
After saying this, he took bread, thanked God in front of everyone, broke it, and began to eat.
Then everyone was encouraged and ate some food too.
There were 276 of us on the ship in all.
After they’d eaten enough, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they didn’t recognize the land, but they saw a bay with a beach and decided to try to run the ship aground there.
They cut loose the anchors and left them in the sea. At the same time, they untied the rudder ropes, hoisted the foresail to the wind, and headed for the beach.
But they hit a sandbar where two currents met and ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and wouldn’t move, while the stern began breaking apart under the force of the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners so none could swim away and escape.
But the centurion wanted to save Paul, so he stopped them. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for land,
and the rest to follow on planks or pieces of the ship. In this way, everyone reached land safely.
After we made it safely to shore, we learned that the island was called Malta.
The local people showed us extraordinary kindness. They lit a fire and welcomed all of us because it was raining and cold.
Paul gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire. A viper, driven out by the heat, latched onto his hand.
When the local people saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to each other, “This man must be a murderer. He escaped the sea, but Justice won’t let him live.”
But Paul shook the snake off into the fire and wasn’t harmed.
They expected him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. After waiting a long time and seeing nothing happen, they changed their minds and said he was a god.
Nearby were lands owned by the island’s leading man, named Publius. He welcomed us and kindly hosted us for three days.
Publius’ father was sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in, prayed, laid his hands on him, and healed him.
After that happened, the rest of the sick people on the island also came and were healed.
They honored us in many ways, and when we sailed, they supplied everything we needed.
After three months, we sailed in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered on the island. Its figurehead showed the Twin Brothers.
We stopped at Syracuse and stayed there for three days.
From there we sailed around the coast and reached Rhegium. The next day a south wind came up, and two days later we arrived at Puteoli,
where we found believers who invited us to stay with them for seven days. Then we went on to Rome.
The believers there had heard about us and came to meet us as far as the Market of Appius and the Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
When we entered Rome, Paul was allowed to live by himself, with a soldier guarding him. The other prisoners were handed over to the captain of the guard.

Three days later, Paul called together the Jewish leaders. When they arrived, he said, “Brothers, I haven’t done anything against our people or the customs of our ancestors. Yet I was handed over as a prisoner in Jerusalem to the Romans,
who examined me and wanted to release me because they found nothing deserving death.
But when the Jews objected, I had to appeal to Caesar—not because I had any charge against my own people.
That’s why I asked to see you and talk with you. I’m wearing this chain because of Israel’s hope.”
They said to him, “We haven’t received any letters from Judea about you, and none of our people who have come here has reported or said anything bad about you.
But we’d like to hear what you think. We know this group is spoken against everywhere.”

They set a day to meet with him, and many people came to where he was staying. From morning until evening he explained God’s Kingdom and tried to persuade them about Jesus, using the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
Some were convinced by what he said, but others didn’t believe.
They couldn’t agree with one another, and they began to leave after Paul made this final statement: “The Holy Spirit spoke rightly through the prophet Isaiah to your ancestors,
saying, ‘Go to this people and tell them: You will hear and hear, but never understand; you will look and look, but never see.

For this people’s heart has become dull. Their ears barely hear, and they have closed their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, turn back, and I would heal them.’”
“So let it be known to you: God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen.”
After he said this, the Jews left, arguing strongly among themselves.
Paul stayed for two full years in a house he rented himself and welcomed everyone who came to him.
He preached God’s Kingdom and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without anyone stopping him.
